# Results — Study 55 (Summer-Lull): "Sell in May" on the S&P 500, 1928–2026

*Generated by [`examples/verify.py`](../examples/verify.py). Monthly total return of the **S&P 500
(^GSPC)**, daily from Yahoo resampled to month-end, 1928–2026 (1,182 months). Winter = Nov–Apr, summer
= May–Oct. As-of 2026-06; inputs fingerprint `b5bbd3b8ce29`.*

## The verdict, earned — Signal `WEAK` · Tradability `MIRAGE` · "Sell in May is good advice"? `NOT SUPPORTED`

The Halloween seasonal is **real and remarkably persistent** — winter months have earned **86 bp/mo
(+5.3%/yr)** against summer's **45 bp/mo (+2.7%/yr)**, a gap that holds in *both* halves of a 98-year
sample. But the gap is only `WEAK` statistically (Welch t **1.3**), and the trading rule is a `MIRAGE`:
"sell in May and go away" matches buy-and-hold's Sharpe (**0.43 vs 0.42**) while compounding to **less
money** (4.5%/yr vs 6.3%) — because summer returns are still **positive**. You'd sit in cash earning
nothing to dodge a season that pays +2.7%/yr. The lower drawdown is just the usual exposure-reduction
illusion. The seasonal is real; "sell in May" is `NOT SUPPORTED`.

## Data stamp

- **Index**: S&P 500 (^GSPC) monthly TR, 1928–2026, 1,182 months, fingerprint `b5bbd3b8ce29`

## Winter really does beat summer — and always has

| | mean | annualised | n |
|---|---|---|---|
| winter (Nov–Apr) | **86 bp/mo** | **+5.3%** | 592 |
| summer (May–Oct) | **45 bp/mo** | **+2.7%** | 590 |
| Welch t (winter − summer) | | **1.3** | |

The pattern is genuine and durable. But a t of 1.3 over a century says the *magnitude* is noisy, and —
crucially — summer is **positive**, not negative. "Sell in May" presumes summer is a season to *avoid*;
it isn't, it's merely a season that pays less.

## …and "sell in May" still loses to doing nothing

| | CAGR | Sharpe | max-DD |
|---|---|---|---|
| Sell-in-May (cash in summer) | +4.5% | **0.43** | −71% |
| Buy & hold | +6.3% | **0.42** | −86% |

Same Sharpe, a third less wealth. The rule's only "benefit" — a shallower drawdown — comes from being
out of the market half the year, exactly the exposure-reduction illusion seen in
[Study 41 Hangover](../../41-hangover/) and [Study 42 Last-Call](../../42-last-call/). Skipping a
positive-return season cannot improve risk-adjusted performance.

## It hasn't decayed — but that doesn't rescue the rule

| | winter | summer |
|---|---|---|
| 1928–1999 | 88 bp/mo | 47 bp/mo |
| 2000–on | 81 bp/mo | 40 bp/mo |

Unusually for a calendar effect, the winter-summer gap persists post-publication (Bouman-Jacobsen 2002).
The seasonal is one of the most robust on the bench — which makes the point sharper: even a *durable*
seasonal doesn't justify the trade, because the "bad" season still makes money.

## The honest takeaway

"Sell in May and go away" rests on a real, persistent seasonal — winter beats summer, for nearly a
century. But it is `WEAK` (t 1.3) and the advice is `NOT SUPPORTED`: summer returns are positive, so
sitting it out just lowers your wealth at the same Sharpe. The right reading isn't "avoid summer" — it's
"summer pays a bit less." A `MIRAGE` to trade, a true fact to know.
